content: 1. In the Philippines, a study published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2001 evaluated the immune responses of dogs to oral rabies vaccines under field conditions. This research provided critical insights into the effectiveness of oral vaccination strategies in real-world settings. 2. In Morocco, the first trials of oral rabies vaccination using SAG2 dog baits were conducted, as reported in Clinical and Experimental Vaccine Research in 2014. These trials demonstrated the feasibility of using oral vaccines to control rabies in dog populations. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidance in 2007 for research and field application of oral rabies vaccines in dogs. This document serves as a comprehensive resource for implementing oral vaccination programs to combat rabies. 4. A field evaluation conducted in Tunisia in 1998 assessed two bait delivery systems for oral immunization of dogs against rabies. The study, published in Vaccine, highlighted the importance of effective bait delivery mechanisms in achieving widespread vaccination coverage. 5. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) Scientific Panel on Animal Health and Welfare (AHAW) provided an update in 2015 on oral vaccination of foxes and raccoon dogs against rabies. This report emphasized the success of oral rabies vaccination campaigns in controlling rabies in wildlife populations. 6. The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) developed model veterinary certificates for the international movement of dogs, cats, and ferrets from rabies-infected countries. These certificates are part of the Terrestrial Animal Health Code and aim to prevent the spread of rabies through animal trade and travel. 7. A review published in Frontiers in Veterinary Science in 2017 examined the role of dog population management in rabies elimination. The study highlighted current approaches and future opportunities for reducing rabies transmission through effective population control measures. 8. The second edition of Dogs, Zoonoses, and Public Health, published by CAB International in 2013, provides a comprehensive overview of the role of dogs in zoonotic disease transmission, including rabies, and strategies for public health interventions. 9. A critical review published in the Journal of Animal Ecology in 2013 evaluated evidence-based control of canine rabies through population density reduction. The findings suggested that reducing host density alone is insufficient for controlling rabies and emphasized the need for integrated approaches. 10. The WHO Technical Report Series No. 1012 (2018) provided an in-depth analysis of rabies epidemiology and ecology in carnivore species. It documented cases of rabies transmission and highlighted the importance of understanding host dynamics for effective disease control. 11. Rabies in bats is a significant concern, as bats are primary hosts for lyssaviruses. The WHO report noted that bats exhibit unique ecological traits, such as long lifespans and low population growth rates, which influence the maintenance and transmission of lyssaviruses. 12. Vampire bat-mediated rabies poses a major public health problem in tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. The common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) is a primary reservoir, frequently transmitting rabies to humans and domestic animals, particularly in remote areas of the Amazon rainforest. 13. Rodents are not primary hosts for rabies and play a negligible role in its transmission. Testing of wild and synanthropic rodents in rabies-endemic areas has revealed only rare instances of spillover infections. 14. Rabies outbreaks in endangered carnivore species, such as Ethiopian wolves and African wild dogs, threaten their conservation. Spillover from domestic dogs is a significant risk, and eliminating dog-mediated rabies would reduce the threat to these vulnerable populations. 15. Wolves, while susceptible to rabies, do not sustain independent transmission cycles due to their low population densities and territorial behavior. Rabies in wolves typically results from spillover infections from other carnivores. 16. Past strategies to control wildlife rabies, such as culling, have proven ineffective and are not recommended. Rabies transmission in wildlife is less density-dependent than previously assumed, and mass vaccination is a more effective and humane control method. 17. Oral rabies vaccination (ORV) strategies have successfully eliminated fox rabies in parts of Europe, Canada, and the USA. These programs rely on safe vaccines, effective bait designs, and automated bait distribution systems. 18. ORV strategies must be tailored to specific wildlife host species. While fox ORV strategies have been adapted for other species like raccoons and coyotes, optimization is required for certain hosts, such as mongooses and skunks. 19. Baits for oral rabies vaccines should be designed to ensure vaccine release onto susceptible tissues, such as the oropharyngeal mucosa or tonsils, to elicit an immune response. Markers like tetracycline can be used to assess vaccine uptake.
